title: Observation of complete delocalization in disordered photonic lattices
comment: Main Text (5 pages, 4 figures); Supplemental Material (11 pages, 10 figures); Supplemental Material is added as an Ancillary file; Comments are welcome
summary: We present the exceptional phenomenon of complete absence of Anderson localization, and perfect transmission of particles, in a completely disordered diamond-dot chain. We analytically show a proof for the condition to observe this exceptional phenomenon, based on a transparent window emerging from a geometrical condition. We support our theoretical prediction by numerical simulations and direct experimental observation of the transmission probabilities of the light in a femtosecond laser-written diamond-dot photonic lattices. We additionally show that for a $π$ effective magnetic flux, extreme localization of the light in the same system may occur, independently on the specific geometry. Our results open up an excellent platform for controlling the transmission of energy from ballistic to zero transmission, in a completely disordered lattice system..

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that Anderson localization can be completely absent in a disordered diamond-dot chain under a specific geometric condition, allowing perfect transmission. Conversely, with a π effective magnetic flux, extreme localization occurs irrespective of geometry. The findings are supported analytically, numerically, and experimentally using femtosecond laser-written photonic lattices.
AI.motivation: To investigate the exceptional phenomenon of complete absence of Anderson localization and perfect transmission in a completely disordered system, challenging the conventional expectation that disorder always induces localization.
AI.method: Analytical proof of a transparent window condition based on geometry, supported by numerical simulations and direct experimental observation of light transmission probabilities in femtosecond laser-written diamond-dot photonic lattices.
AI.result: Perfect transmission (absence of Anderson localization) occurs under a specific geometric condition; a π effective magnetic flux induces extreme localization independent of geometry, enabling control from ballistic to zero transmission.
AI.conclusion: The diamond-dot chain provides an excellent platform for controlling energy transmission from ballistic to zero transmission in a completely disordered lattice system.

title: Truncated Wigner dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses
summary: Quantum spin glasses are often considered testbeds for studying quantum optimization algorithms and as such have been the subject of various quantum advantage claims. Here we investigate the near adiabatic dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses within the (discrete) truncated Wigner approximation (TWA). Benchmarks on small systems show that TWA recovers sample-to-sample fluctuations of the Edwards-Anderson order parameter, over a wide range of annealing times, with increasing fidelity when the system size increases. We extract critical exponents from the Binder cumulant in line with theoretical expectations, reproducing recent quantum experiments. The computational cost of the method is minimal and it can easily be applied to tens of thousands of qubits.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the truncated Wigner approximation (TWA) to study near-adiabatic dynamics in biclique quantum spin glasses. TWA accurately captures sample-to-sample fluctuations and critical exponents with minimal computational cost, scaling to tens of thousands of qubits.
AI.motivation: Quantum spin glasses serve as testbeds for quantum optimization algorithms and have been central to quantum advantage claims; understanding their dynamics efficiently is crucial for benchmarking.
AI.method: The study employs the discrete truncated Wigner approximation (TWA) to simulate near-adiabatic dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses, benchmarking against small systems for fidelity and scaling to large qubit counts.
AI.result: TWA recovers sample-to-sample fluctuations of the Edwards-Anderson order parameter with increasing fidelity as system size grows, extracts critical exponents from the Binder cumulant matching theoretical expectations and recent quantum experiments, and achieves minimal computational cost applicable to tens of thousands of qubits.
AI.conclusion: The TWA method is an efficient and scalable tool for studying quantum spin glass dynamics, reproducing experimental results and enabling large-scale simulations without prohibitive computational overhead.

title: Solving Nonequilibrium Dynamics via Influence Matrix Bootstrap: Floquet-PXP Model
summary: Studies of integrable systems have profoundly deepened the fundamental understanding of quantum many-body physics. While equilibrium properties such as ground states and thermodynamics can often be characterized efficiently, accurately characterizing nonequilibrium integrable dynamics remains a significant challenge. Here, we address this problem in the "Rule 201" quantum cellular automaton, an integrable Trotterization of the PXP Hamiltonian. Using the tensor-network approach of the influence matrix, we develop local conditions called generalized zipper conditions that allow exact solutions of local dynamics. We also introduce a numerical bootstrap method for solving influence matrices with finite but relatively large bond dimensions. This uncovers a rich landscape of nonequilibrium behavior exhibiting initial-state dependence. As an example, we investigate the fate of persistent oscillating dynamics under local non-integrable perturbations, and present analytical results for non-thermal relaxation constrained by conservation laws. We also obtain numerically exact results for entanglement growth across a broad class of initial states. Furthermore, from an information-theoretic perspective, we identify a refined structure of multitime correlations termed the hidden Markov order: the memory encoded in the dynamics separates into finite-length and long-range distributed components, which becomes transparent in an exact split-index matrix-product-state representation of the influence matrix. Our approach enables unified investigations of nonthermalizing and thermalizing regimes of nonequilibrium dynamics within a single analytically tractable model, and can be tested experimentally in state-of-the-art quantum simulators such as Rydberg atom arrays.

AI.tldr: The paper develops exact solutions and numerical bootstrap methods for nonequilibrium dynamics in the integrable "Rule 201" quantum cellular automaton using influence matrix tensor networks. It uncovers initial-state-dependent dynamics, analyzes persistent oscillations under perturbations, and identifies a hidden Markov order structure in multitime correlations, enabling unified study of nonthermalizing and thermalizing regimes.
AI.motivation: Characterizing nonequilibrium integrable quantum dynamics remains a significant challenge even though equilibrium properties are well understood.
AI.method: The authors use the tensor-network influence matrix approach to develop generalized zipper conditions for exact local dynamics, and introduce a numerical bootstrap method for solving influence matrices with finite bond dimensions.
AI.result: They uncover initial-state-dependent nonequilibrium behavior, obtain analytical results for non-thermal relaxation under perturbations, numerically exact entanglement growth across many initial states, and identify a hidden Markov order structure in multitime correlations via an exact split-index matrix-product-state representation.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables unified analytical investigations of nonthermalizing and thermalizing nonequilibrium dynamics within a single tractable model, with experimental testability in quantum simulators like Rydberg atom arrays.

title: Indefinite Quantum Causality
comment: 76 pages + a 2-pages Appendix; 32 figures + 1 in the Appendix
summary: In recent years, operational approaches to quantum foundations have been developed as a means of understanding the core principles and distinctive features of quantum theory. Such approaches typically view physical processes as sequences of operations, with earlier operations serving as causes of later effects. However, a growing literature is emerging on the possibility of relaxing this assumption and allowing for quantum indefiniteness in the causal order. This development stems from a variety of motivations, both fundamental and applied, including exploring the role of causality in quantum theory, the interplay between quantum theory and general relativity, and higher-order quantum computing. A prominent offshoot of this development is the emergence of indefinite causal order as a feasible resource for quantum information processing. This review provides an overview of the current state of the art in the field, covering the methodology underlying indefinite quantum causality within the so-called "process matrix formalism", outlining key results and experimental implementations, and discussing recent advances.

AI.tldr: This review covers the process matrix formalism and operational approaches to indefinite causal order in quantum theory, including key results, experimental implementations, and recent advances, highlighting its role as a resource for quantum information processing.
AI.motivation: To understand the core principles of quantum theory by relaxing the assumption of fixed causal order, exploring the interplay between quantum theory and general relativity, and investigating indefinite causal order as a resource for quantum information processing.
AI.method: The review is based on the process matrix formalism, an operational framework that describes physical processes as sequences of operations without assuming a predefined causal order, allowing for quantum indefiniteness in causality.
AI.result: Indefinite causal order has emerged as a feasible resource for quantum information processing, with key theoretical results and experimental implementations demonstrating its viability.
AI.conclusion: The field of indefinite quantum causality, as articulated through the process matrix formalism, represents a mature area of research with both foundational implications and practical applications in quantum information processing.

title: Efficient classical representation and quantum state preparation of complete active space wavefunctions
summary: Quantum computers promise to solve the electronic structure problem for a large class of molecules. However, the performance of relevant quantum algorithms hinges on preparing initial states with substantial overlap with the target eigenvector. For classically challenging molecules with strong electron correlation, starting from multi-reference states, such as complete active space (CAS) wavefunctions is necessary. Unfortunately, the most advanced state preparation protocols applied to such states result in a gate complexity that scales exponentially with the active space size $d$. In fact, even encoding a CAS state classically is traditionally believed to be intractable for chemically relevant systems. Here, we draw insights from the recently introduced Quantum Paldus Transform (QPT) to show that there exists an efficient classical representation of CAS states and to design a new state preparation routine outperforming previous ones. The QPT represents a transformation from the Fock basis to a friendlier symmetry-adapted basis. Our main contribution consists in showing that CAS states expanded in this basis can efficiently be represented as a matrix product state (MPS) with a bond dimension scaling as $O(d^2)$. One can then efficiently load the MPS on a quantum computer and use the inverse QPT to transform the state to the Fock basis. Moreover, our method can easily be extended to the efficient preparation of CAS states in first quantisation with similar complexity. Crucially, we demonstrate that the complexity of both state preparation protocols only grows polynomially as $O(d^3)$ , which constitutes to the best of our knowledge an exponential improvement over the state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an efficient classical representation of complete active space (CAS) states using the Quantum Paldus Transform (QPT), enabling matrix product state (MPS) representation with bond dimension O(d²) and state preparation with O(d³) gate complexity—an exponential improvement over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Quantum algorithms for electronic structure problems require initial states with high overlap with target eigenvectors. For strongly correlated molecules, multi-reference CAS states are necessary, but existing state preparation protocols have exponential gate complexity in active space size d, and CAS states themselves are traditionally considered intractable to represent classically.
AI.method: The method leverages the Quantum Paldus Transform (QPT) to map from the Fock basis to a symmetry-adapted basis. CAS states expanded in this basis are efficiently represented as matrix product states (MPS) with bond dimension O(d²). The MPS is loaded onto a quantum computer, then the inverse QPT transforms the state back to the Fock basis. The approach also extends to first quantization.
AI.result: Both state preparation protocols scale polynomially as O(d³), representing an exponential improvement over the state of the art (previously exponential in d).
AI.conclusion: The work shows that CAS states can be represented classically efficiently and that their quantum state preparation can be done with polynomial complexity, significantly advancing the feasibility of quantum algorithms for strongly correlated molecular systems.

title: Quantum deformations of $\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R}))$. Part I: Fidelity and experimental benchmarking
summary: This work explores the effects of both the standard quantum $q$-deformation and the non-standard $h$-deformation of the Hopf algebra $\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R}))$ on multi-qubit systems. By constructing the states of a Hilbert space of $N$ qubits through the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients associated with the deformed algebras, we show that these states naturally coincide with the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian of the $q$- and $h$-deformed Kittel-Shore models. We compare the resulting deformed states with those typically targeted in quantum information experiments, providing a bridge between algebraic constructions and experimentally relevant quantum resources. Fidelities with respect to the undeformed states are computed to establish how the quantum correlations are affected, both for few-qubit systems (including Dicke and non-Dicke states), and in the macroscopic limit ($N \to \infty$) through closed-form formulas derived for arbitrary Dicke states. The results reveal different behaviors between the two deformations. The $q$-deformation smoothly modifies the states and maintains a residual overlap with the original configurations, while the $h$-deformation rapidly makes the states orthogonal to their undeformed counterparts. Both models demand a standard $N^{-1}$ rescaling to preserve fidelity stability in the macroscopic limit.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how quantum $q$- and $h$-deformations of the $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ Hopf algebra affect multi-qubit systems, showing that deformed states correspond to eigenstates of deformed Kittel-Shore models. The $q$-deformation smoothly modifies states while $h$-deformation rapidly orthogonalizes them, and both require $N^{-1}$ rescaling for macroscopic fidelity stability.
AI.motivation: To bridge algebraic deformations of Hopf algebras with experimentally relevant quantum resources by exploring how $q$- and $h$-deformations alter multi-qubit quantum correlations and state structures.
AI.method: Construct Hilbert spaces of $N$ qubits using Clebsch-Gordan coefficients of $q$- and $h$-deformed $\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R}))$, map them to eigenstates of deformed Kittel-Shore Hamiltonians, and compute fidelities analytically for arbitrary Dicke states in both finite and macroscopic ($N\to\infty$) regimes.
AI.result: $q$-deformation smoothly alters states preserving residual overlap with undeformed states; $h$-deformation rapidly orthogonalizes states. Both require $N^{-1}$ rescaling to maintain fidelity in the macroscopic limit. Closed-form fidelity formulas are derived for arbitrary Dicke states.
AI.conclusion: The two deformations produce qualitatively different behaviors in quantum correlations, with $q$-deformation offering a tunable, smooth modification suitable for gradual state engineering, while $h$-deformation leads to abrupt orthogonality. The $N^{-1}$ rescaling condition is essential for macroscopic consistency.

title: Local controllability of heralded quantum linear optics
summary: Photonic linear optical networks provide a versatile platform for quantum information processing and quantum state engineering. However, the set of states that can be generated using passive linear optics alone is fundamentally constrained by bosonic symmetries. Heralding, based on conditional measurements on auxiliary modes, is a widely used technique to overcome these limitations and effectively enlarge the set of accessible states. Despite the widespread use of heralding, it is often unclear how specific ancillary resources impact the overall reachability of the target space. In this work, we investigate the local controllability of photonic states in linear optical networks by analyzing the rank of the Jacobian of the output state with respect to the underlying unitary circuit, which provides a quantitative measure of the dimension of the accessible tangent space at a given configuration. Our analysis ranges from passive linear optics to heralded linear optics, where auxiliary resources and conditional measurements are included. Within this framework, we quantify how different resources enlarge the locally accessible state space beyond that of passive linear optics and determine the resources required for the Jacobian rank to reach its maximal value, thereby achieving full local controllability. As maximal local rank is a necessary condition for global reachability, our framework offers a systematic tool to assess and compare the accessible state space of measurement-based photonic architectures, and to establish practical criteria for the resources needed in high-dimensional quantum state engineering.

AI.tldr: This work investigates local controllability of photonic states in linear optical networks by analyzing the Jacobian rank of the output state with respect to the unitary circuit. It quantifies how heralding and auxiliary resources expand the accessible state space beyond passive linear optics, and establishes criteria for achieving full local controllability (maximal Jacobian rank) as a necessary condition for global reachability.
AI.motivation: Heralding is widely used to overcome the limitations of passive linear optics imposed by bosonic symmetries, but it is often unclear how specific ancillary resources impact the overall reachability of the target state space. This work aims to systematically quantify and compare the accessible state space in measurement-based photonic architectures.
AI.method: The authors analyze the rank of the Jacobian of the output state with respect to the underlying unitary circuit, providing a quantitative measure of the dimension of the accessible tangent space at a given configuration. They extend this analysis from passive linear optics to heralded linear optics, incorporating auxiliary resources and conditional measurements.
AI.result: The framework quantifies how different resources (auxiliary modes, heralding) enlarge the locally accessible state space beyond passive linear optics. It determines the resources required for the Jacobian rank to reach its maximal value, thereby achieving full local controllability.
AI.conclusion: Maximal local rank (full local controllability) is a necessary condition for global reachability. The framework provides a systematic tool to assess and compare accessible state spaces of measurement-based photonic architectures and establishes practical criteria for resources needed in high-dimensional quantum state engineering.

title: Nearest-neighbour gates are all you need: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes on a planar grid
summary: High-performance quantum low-density parity-check codes promise substantial reductions in the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation, but most constructions require long-range connectivity or qubit shuttling, both of which are difficult to realise in superconducting architectures. Here we introduce a family of quantum low-density parity-check codes that, for the first time, combines planar open-boundary layouts, finite-size advantages over surface codes, and syndrome extraction using only nearest-neighbour gates on a square grid of qubits. The key idea is to generate check-data connectivity dynamically: nearest-neighbour iSWAP walks both define the stabiliser supports and implement their measurement, avoiding the need for a long-range hardware graph. The resulting circuits achieve optimal constant-depth stabiliser measurement, independent of code size, and naturally remove leakage from the system by exchanging the role of check and data qubits at each syndrome extraction round. We find finite-size instances such as a [[323,14,15]] code, whose code-efficiency ratio is nearly an order of magnitude larger than that of rotated surface-code patches. At around 30 circuit qubits per logical qubit, the best directional tile-code layouts reduce the per-logical per-round logical error rate by up to a factor of 1000 relative to rotated surface-code memories. These results show that the advantages of quantum low-density parity-check codes can survive compilation into strictly planar nearest-neighbour circuits, bringing low-overhead fault-tolerant memories closer to near-term hardware.

AI.tldr: A family of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced that achieves planar nearest-neighbour layouts, optimal constant-depth syndrome extraction via iSWAP walks, and finite-size advantages over surface codes, with a [[323,14,15]] code showing nearly 10× better code-efficiency and up to 1000× lower logical error rate.
AI.motivation: To realize high-performance quantum LDPC codes on superconducting architectures without requiring long-range connectivity or qubit shuttling, which are difficult to implement in practice.
AI.method: Introduces tile codes with dynamic check-data connectivity generated by nearest-neighbour iSWAP walks, which simultaneously define stabiliser supports and implement their measurement in optimal constant-depth circuits, while naturally removing leakage via role exchange.
AI.result: A [[323,14,15]] code with nearly 10× better code-efficiency than rotated surface codes; at ~30 qubits per logical qubit, directional tile-code layouts reduce per-logical per-round logical error rate by up to 1000× compared to rotated surface-code memories.
AI.conclusion: Quantum LDPC code advantages survive compilation into strictly planar nearest-neighbour circuits, bringing low-overhead fault-tolerant memories closer to near-term hardware.

title: Optimal Ansatz-free Hamiltonian Learning In Situ
summary: Characterizing the features of a Hamiltonian that governs a quantum system serves as a fundamental subroutine of quantum device calibration, signal sensing, and error correction. Recent works proposed protocols have achieved the optimal Heisenberg-limited scaling learning ansatz-free Hamiltonians from their real-time evolutions without fully specifying interaction structures. However, these protocols rely on both deep circuits with interleaving probes and control, and extremely short time resolution, making them difficult to implement on near- and intermediate-term in situ quantum experiments. In this work, we propose a computationally efficient, control-free, and ancilla-free algorithm that uses only Pauli product state preparation and measurement, and learns an ansatz-free Hamiltonian $H$ with $||H||\leqΛ$ in total evolution time of $Θ(\fracΛ{ε^2}\log(\fracΛε))$. The evolution time cost of our algorithm is optimal for any control-free protocols as we further prove a lower bound of $Ω(\fracΛ{ε^2}\log(\fracΛε))$. Technically, our method introduces a randomized-sampling framework that combines band-limited kernel-based time sampling with a displacement sieve for Hamiltonian structure learning. The characteristic probe time resolution depends only on $Λ$ instead of $\varepsilon$, which makes our protocol especially appealing in the high-precision regime for sensing and calibration applications. We also show that the algorithm maintains the same asymptotic total evolution time in the presence of state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) noise when the Hamiltonian is local after calibration. Our results demonstrate the fundamental cost of experimentally friendly Hamiltonian learning and provide a practical route to rigorous in situ characterization of near-term quantum platforms.

AI.tldr: A control-free, ancilla-free Hamiltonian learning algorithm using only Pauli product state preparation and measurement achieves optimal Heisenberg-limited scaling with total evolution time Θ(Λ/ε² log(Λ/ε)), matching a proved lower bound for control-free protocols, and uses a randomized-sampling framework with band-limited kernel-based time sampling and displacement sieve.
AI.motivation: Existing optimal Hamiltonian learning protocols achieve Heisenberg-limited scaling but require deep circuits with interleaving probes and control, plus extremely short time resolution, making them impractical for near- and intermediate-term in situ quantum experiments. A more experimentally friendly approach is needed.
AI.method: A randomized-sampling framework combining band-limited kernel-based time sampling with a displacement sieve for Hamiltonian structure learning. It uses only Pauli product state preparation and measurement, requires no control or ancilla, and the characteristic probe time resolution depends only on Λ (the Hamiltonian norm bound) rather than ε (the precision).
AI.result: Achieves total evolution time Θ(Λ/ε² log(Λ/ε)), which is optimal for control-free protocols as proven by a matching lower bound Ω(Λ/ε² log(Λ/ε)). The algorithm maintains the same asymptotic total evolution time even under SPAM noise when the Hamiltonian is local after calibration.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the fundamental cost of experimentally friendly Hamiltonian learning and provide a practical route to rigorous in situ characterization of near-term quantum platforms, being especially appealing for high-precision sensing and calibration applications.

title: Entanglement Scaling and Problem Structure in Quantum Approximate and Adiabatic Optimization Algorithms
summary: Entanglement is widely regarded as a key resource underlying the power of quantum algorithms and their potential to achieve quantum advantage. With the emergence of variational quantum algorithms, however, questions have arisen regarding how entanglement relates to problem structure and algorithmic performance in near-term quantum applications. Here, we examine this relationship through the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), a specific class of variational algorithms, applied to the MaxCut problem. We show that suboptimal variational parameter training can significantly modify the observed entanglement profile, obscuring its scaling behavior. By employing a high-performance optimizer, we find empirical evidence that QAOA exhibits entanglement scaling consistent with that of fermionic Gaussian states (up to a scaling factor) across a broad range of MaxCut instances. We further compare these results with adiabatic quantum computation, observing annealing-schedule-dependent entanglement profiles whose scaling behavior differs markedly from that of QAOA. Together, these findings provide new insight into how entanglement manifests in and distinguishes these two algorithmic paradigms, highlighting its connection to both computational performance and application structure.

AI.tldr: This study examines entanglement scaling in QAOA for MaxCut, finding that suboptimal training obscures entanglement behavior, but with high-performance optimization, QAOA exhibits entanglement scaling similar to fermionic Gaussian states. The entanglement profiles differ markedly from those in adiabatic quantum computation, providing insights into how entanglement distinguishes these algorithmic paradigms.
AI.motivation: To understand how entanglement relates to problem structure and algorithmic performance in near-term variational quantum algorithms, specifically QAOA applied to MaxCut.
AI.method: Applied QAOA to MaxCut problems, comparing entanglement profiles under suboptimal vs. high-performance optimizers, and contrasted results with adiabatic quantum computation entanglement scaling.
AI.result: Suboptimal training modifies entanglement profiles; with high-performance optimization, QAOA entanglement scales like fermionic Gaussian states; adiabatic quantum computation shows markedly different annealing-schedule-dependent entanglement scaling.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement manifests differently in QAOA vs. adiabatic quantum computation, with distinct scaling behaviors highlighting connections between entanglement, computational performance, and algorithmic structure.

title: Exact Markovian Dissipation Requires Singular Energy Resources
summary: The Gorini--Kossakowski--Lindblad--Sudarshan (GKLS) equation describes irreversible quantum dynamical semigroups. We show that this description cannot be exact under physically regular energy conditions. We prove that the open-system survival probability under physically regular energy conditions has sublinear decay, whereas any dissipative GKLS semigroup has a linear short-time decay. Hence exact Markovian dissipation requires singular energy resources: an unbounded-below total Hamiltonian or infinite initial energy, and a divergent interaction-energy moment. Therefore, a dissipative time-independent GKLS equation should be regarded as an effective description rather than the exact reduced dynamics of a Hamiltonian dilation satisfying physically regular energy conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that exact GKLS (Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan) master equation dynamics, which describes irreversible quantum Markovian processes, cannot be realized under physically regular energy conditions because GKLS predicts linear short-time decay while physical open systems with bounded-below Hamiltonians exhibit sublinear decay. Therefore, Markovian dissipation requires singular energy resources, and GKLS should only be treated as an effective, not exact, description.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the GKLS equation, the standard framework for Markovian open quantum systems, can be an exact description of reduced dynamics under physically plausible energy conditions, or whether it must be regarded as an approximation.
AI.method: The authors compare the short-time decay behavior of the survival probability: they prove that under physically regular energy conditions (bounded-below total Hamiltonian, finite initial energy, finite interaction-energy moment), the survival probability exhibits sublinear decay, whereas any dissipative GKLS semigroup inevitably yields linear short-time decay. The contradiction shows that exact GKLS dynamics require singular energy resources.
AI.result: Exact Markovian dissipation described by a time-independent GKLS equation is incompatible with physically regular energy conditions. To achieve exact GKLS dynamics, the system would need an unbounded-below Hamiltonian, infinite initial energy, or divergent interaction-energy moments.
AI.conclusion: The dissipative time-independent GKLS equation should be regarded as an effective (approximate) description rather than the exact reduced dynamics derived from a Hamiltonian dilation satisfying physically regular energy conditions.

title: Distinguishing quantum processes with bounded coherent memory
summary: Distinguishing multi-time quantum processes is a fundamental task underlying the diagnosis, benchmarking, and learning of temporally correlated quantum dynamics. The standard benchmark for distinguishing two processes is the strategy-norm distance, which optimizes over arbitrary adaptive probing strategies but can require large coherent memory and time-dependent control. We introduce machines for autonomous distinction~($\mathsf{MAD}$s): probing strategies that apply the same quantum instrument at each time step, retain the full classical outcome record, and carry a coherent memory of dimension $d_A$. Optimizing over these strategies defines a memory-parametrized distinguishability measure, $d^{(N)}_{\mathsf{MAD}}(\mathbf{P}^N,\mathbf{Q}^N;d_A)$. We show that the resulting hierarchy is monotone in coherent memory and complete at finite times. Specifically, any admissible $N$-step probing strategy can be compiled into a single $\mathsf{MAD}$ with an internal counter and sufficiently large coherent memory, so the hierarchy saturates the strategy-norm benchmark. For recurrent processes generated by repeated system--environment interactions, we derive a single-step description that separates the generation of new distinguishing information from the propagation and decay of information generated at earlier times. Numerical results in a repeated-interaction model show that increasing coherent memory systematically improves the $\mathsf{MAD}$ success probability and closes the gap to the strategy-norm distance while remaining substantially more tractable to evaluate. $\mathsf{MAD}$ distinguishability therefore provides an operational and scalable framework for quantifying what can be learned about genuinely multi-time quantum processes with bounded coherent memory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Machines for Autonomous Distinction (MADs)—probing strategies using identical quantum instruments at each step with classical records and bounded coherent memory—to define a memory-parametrized distinguishability measure for multi-time quantum processes. This measure forms a monotone hierarchy that saturates the strategy-norm distance at finite times, is tractable, and separates information generation from memory propagation in recurrent dynamics.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing multi-time quantum processes is essential for diagnosing, benchmarking, and learning temporally correlated quantum dynamics. The standard strategy-norm distance benchmark requires arbitrary adaptive strategies with large coherent memory and time-dependent control, which are experimentally demanding. The authors aim to develop a more tractable yet operational framework that quantifies distinguishability under realistic coherent memory constraints.
AI.method: The authors define Machines for Autonomous Distinction (MADs): probing strategies that apply the same quantum instrument at each time step, retain full classical outcomes, and carry a coherent memory of dimension d_A. They optimize over such strategies to define a memory-parametrized distinguishability measure d^{(N)}_{MAD}. They prove the resulting hierarchy is monotone in coherent memory and complete at finite times, show that any N-step strategy compiles into a single MAD with a counter and sufficient memory, and derive a single-step description for recurrent processes that separates information generation from propagation/decay.
AI.result: The hierarchy is monotone in coherent memory and saturates the strategy-norm benchmark at finite times. For recurrent processes, a single-step description separates new distinguishing information from propagated information. Numerical results in a repeated-interaction model show that increasing coherent memory systematically improves MAD success probability and closes the gap to the strategy-norm distance, while remaining substantially more tractable to evaluate.
AI.conclusion: MAD distinguishability provides an operational and scalable framework for quantifying what can be learned about genuinely multi-time quantum processes under bounded coherent memory constraints, bridging theoretical optimality and practical implementability.

title: Complexity of detecting large coefficients in the Pauli basis
summary: We study the problem of deciding, given a mechanism to prepare a quantum state $ρ$ and a value $\varepsilon > 0$, whether there is some non-identity Pauli matrix $P$ such that $|Tr(P ρ)| \geq \varepsilon$. We consider that the state $ρ$ is described as the result of tracing out some of the qubits of a pure state prepared by a circuit $C$, and we assume the promise that either there is a Pauli matrix satisfying the stated condition or, instead, that for all non-identity Pauli matrices $P$ it is the case that $|Tr(Pρ)|\leq \varepsilon/2$. The problem is in $QCMA$, and we prove that if it belongs to $BQP$ then $NP \subseteq BQP$. The result is obtained through a reduction from the minimum-weight code problem, and it holds even when $ρ$ is assumed to be a pure state (i.e. when no qubits are discarded) and $\varepsilon$ is constant. This resolves an open question regarding the existence of efficient tomographic procedures to find the largest coefficients of a quantum state in the Pauli basis: namely, they do not exist under the standard hypothesis $NP \nsubseteq BQP$.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that deciding whether a quantum state has a large Pauli coefficient is QCMA-complete, and if it were in BQP, then NP ⊆ BQP, implying no efficient Pauli-basis tomography exists under standard complexity assumptions.
AI.motivation: To determine whether efficient quantum algorithms exist for finding large Pauli coefficients of a quantum state — a task relevant to quantum state tomography and property testing.
AI.method: A reduction from the minimum-weight code problem (NP-hard) to the Pauli coefficient decision problem, using circuits that prepare pure states and constant ε.
AI.result: The problem is in QCMA, and membership in BQP would imply NP ⊆ BQP, making it unlikely under standard complexity hypotheses. This holds even for pure states and constant ε.
AI.conclusion: Efficient tomographic procedures to find the largest Pauli coefficients of a quantum state do not exist unless NP ⊆ BQP, resolving an open question.

title: Passive-User Bell-State Loop-Back Key Establishment without Quantum Detectors at the User Nodes
summary: We propose and analyze a Bell-state extension of the Loop-Back quantum key distribution architecture for secret-key establishment between two passive users that do not require quantum transmitters or quantum detectors. In the proposed setting, a single active station, Alice, provides the entangled-state infrastructure, retains one qubit of an initially prepared Bell pair, and sends the traveling subsystem through two passive users, denoted by $B_1$ and $B_2$. Each passive user applies a local Pauli operation to the same traveling subsystem, so that the operation observed by Alice is only the effective composition $U_{\mathrm{eff}}=U_2U_1$. After the subsystem returns, Alice performs a Bell-state measurement and, using her private knowledge of the initial Bell state, deterministically identifies the effective Pauli operation. However, the individual factors $U_1$ and $U_2$ remain algebraically hidden from Alice whenever the local choices are uniformly and independently selected. The public effective operation acts as a parity-like constraint: each passive user can infer the operation applied by the other from its own private choice, while the active station learns only the global composition. This construction transfers the essential distributed-transformation mechanism of passive-user Loop-Back QKD to the entangled-state regime. Unlike single-qubit passive-user schemes, whose useful events are intrinsically post-selected, the Bell-state version is limited primarily by the success probability of the Bell-state measurement. We discuss the algebraic structure of the protocol, its interpretation as an infrastructure-assisted mediated key-establishment mechanism, and the physical assumptions required to protect passive Pauli modulators against active injection or Trojan-horse-type attacks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Bell-state extension of Loop-Back QKD, where a single active station (Alice) prepares Bell pairs and sends one qubit through two passive users (B1, B2) who apply local Pauli operations. Alice performs a Bell-state measurement to identify the effective composite operation, while individual operations remain hidden. Each passive user infers the other's operation from its own, enabling secret-key establishment.
AI.motivation: To extend the passive-user Loop-Back QKD architecture to the entangled-state regime, enabling secret-key establishment between two passive users (no quantum transmitters/detectors) using Bell states rather than single-qubit post-selected schemes, thereby improving efficiency by replacing post-selection with Bell-state measurement success probability as the primary limitation.
AI.method: Alice prepares a Bell pair, retains one qubit, and sends the other through two passive users sequentially. Each user applies a local Pauli operation (U1, U2) independently and uniformly. Alice performs a Bell-state measurement on the returned qubit and her retained qubit, deterministically identifying the effective composite operation U_eff = U2U1, while individual factors remain hidden.
AI.result: The protocol transfers the distributed-transformation mechanism of single-qubit passive-user Loop-Back QKD to the entangled-state regime. Unlike single-qubit schemes limited by post-selection, this Bell-state version is limited primarily by the success probability of the Bell-state measurement. The public effective operation acts as a parity-like constraint enabling key inference.
AI.conclusion: The Bell-state extension provides an infrastructure-assisted mediated key-establishment mechanism for two passive users, with improved efficiency over single-qubit schemes, requiring analysis of physical assumptions to protect passive Pauli modulators against active injection or Trojan-horse attacks.

title: Electrical Noise Produced by Micron-Sized Particles above a Surface Paul Trap
summary: Electric field noise produced by the surface of ion trap electrodes reduces the fidelity of quantum computing operations. Despite decades of investigation its microscopic origins remain unclear. Here, we measure electric field noise at trapping locations along the symmetry axis of a linear surface Paul trap. We find that noise levels vary by three orders-of-magnitude in one 600$\,μ$m section of the trap. Optical and scanning electron microscope images show micron-sized particles close to the trapping locations with the highest noise levels. We find that modeling the particles as a lossy dielectric with a effective loss tangent $\tanθ=0.33(0.06)$ describes the magnitude of the noise, as well as its spatial and frequency dependence. Our observations may explain the large variation of reported noise levels in literature.

AI.tldr: Electric field noise from surface ion trap electrodes varies by three orders of magnitude within a 600 μm section, linked to micron-sized particles near high-noise trapping locations. Modeling particles as lossy dielectrics (tanθ=0.33±0.06) explains noise magnitude, spatial, and frequency dependence, potentially explaining literature variation.
AI.motivation: Electric field noise from ion trap electrode surfaces degrades quantum computing fidelity, but its microscopic origins have remained unclear despite decades of research.
AI.method: Measured electric field noise along the symmetry axis of a linear surface Paul trap; used optical and SEM imaging to identify micron-sized particles; modeled particles as lossy dielectrics with an effective loss tangent.
AI.result: Noise levels vary by three orders of magnitude in a 600 μm section; micron-sized particles found near highest-noise locations; model with loss tangent tanθ=0.33(0.06) matches noise magnitude, spatial, and frequency dependence.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that surface contaminants (micron-sized particles) are a dominant source of electric field noise, potentially explaining the wide variation in reported noise levels across different experiments.

title: Emergency hub placement with a neutral-atom quantum computer
summary: We study the problem of emergency operation center placement in disaster response, where a minimal number of hubs must be selected to ensure timely coverage of all affected locations. This task can be formulated as a minimum dominating set problem on a graph encoding reachability within a target response time. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical approximation framework that leverages neutral-atom quantum computers as independent set samplers. Candidate dominating sets are constructed from both small maximal independent sets and complements of large independent sets, and are subsequently refined via a lightweight classical procedure. We benchmark the approach on synthetic instances and realistic case studies, and implement it on the Fresnel quantum processor by Pasqal, solving instances of up to 100 nodes. Our results show that quantum-generated samples, despite hardware noise, enable near-optimal solutions of the placement problem. Overall, our results demonstrate that neutral-atom devices operating in analog mode can already be used to tackle graph optimization problems for real-world applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical framework using neutral-atom quantum computers to solve the minimum dominating set problem for emergency operation center placement, achieving near-optimal solutions on instances up to 100 nodes using Pasqal's Fresnel processor.
AI.motivation: Emergency operation center placement requires selecting a minimal set of hubs to ensure timely coverage of all affected locations during disaster response, which can be formulated as a minimum dominating set problem on a reachability graph.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum-classical framework leveraging neutral-atom quantum computers as independent set samplers. Candidate dominating sets are constructed from small maximal independent sets and complements of large independent sets, then refined via lightweight classical post-processing.
AI.result: Benchmarked on synthetic instances and realistic case studies, implemented on Pasqal's Fresnel quantum processor for up to 100 nodes. Quantum-generated samples, despite hardware noise, yield near-optimal solutions.
AI.conclusion: Neutral-atom devices operating in analog mode can already tackle graph optimization problems for real-world applications like disaster response placement.

title: Stalls and Spequlation: Pipelined Execution for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computation
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires the coordinated action of three distinct systems: classical control logic, quantum hardware, and classical error decoders. Current scheduling models treat logical operations as atomic, hiding the fact that these subsystems operate sequentially and spend significant time idle. We present a pipelined execution framework that decomposes each logical operation into its component stages i.e. Control, Execute, and Decode. Building on this, we discuss some speculation strategies that allow successor operations to begin processing before their predecessors have completed decoding. We evaluate our framework on several common benchmarks and show that pipelining with speculation reduces total pipeline steps by 20-40% compared to a no-speculation baseline. The most aggressive strategy consistently outperforms conservative alternatives, even though partial rollback is needed at times, because the per-rollback penalty is small relative to the parallelism gained. We further show that speculation facilitates load balancing by distributing work more evenly across the heterogeneous subsystems of a fault-tolerant quantum computer, converting idle time into useful computation while also saving on execution time.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a pipelined execution framework for fault-tolerant quantum computation that decomposes logical operations into Control, Execute, and Decode stages. Using speculation strategies to start successor operations before predecessors finish decoding, the approach reduces pipeline steps by 20-40%, improves load balancing across subsystems, and converts idle time into useful computation despite occasional rollback penalties.
AI.motivation: Current scheduling models treat logical operations as atomic, hiding the sequential nature and idle time of the three subsystems (classical control logic, quantum hardware, and error decoders) in fault-tolerant quantum computation.
AI.method: The authors propose a pipelined execution framework that decomposes each logical operation into Control, Execute, and Decode stages, and introduce speculation strategies that allow successor operations to begin before predecessors complete decoding.
AI.result: Pipelining with speculation reduces total pipeline steps by 20-40% compared to a no-speculation baseline. The most aggressive speculation strategy consistently outperforms conservative alternatives, even with occasional partial rollback, as the rollback penalty is small relative to the parallelism gained. Speculation also improves load balancing across heterogeneous subsystems.
AI.conclusion: Speculative pipelining effectively reduces idle time and improves throughput in fault-tolerant quantum computation by exposing subsystem-level parallelism, with rollback costs being outweighed by the benefits of increased parallelism and better load distribution.

title: String dynamics of a (2+1)D U(1) quantum link model on a digital quantum computer
summary: The (2+1)D U(1) pure gauge theory always exists in the confining phase, with strings of non-zero string tension giving a characteristic linear potential between static charges. This makes it a useful testing ground for quantum computing methods designed to study string dynamics of confining gauge theories. Here we implement a minimal U(1) quantum link model on a quantum computer with qubit degrees of freedom representing the dual height variables of the model. This facilitates an efficient realization of plaquette interactions and enables effective calculations of real-time dynamics that are inaccessible to traditional quantum Monte Carlo. A specifically tailored lattice geometry is chosen to match the heavy-hexagonal geometry of the IBM quantum hardware used here, minimizing non-adjacent qubit interactions. By performing quantum quenches from a simple initial string state, we probe the transverse quantum fluctuations of the string before it thermalizes. Our experimental results from digital quantum simulations, with up to 112 qubits, show good agreement with reference tensor-network calculations at short times and with thermal averages at long times. Near the phase transition, the quench dynamics exhibit large fluctuations of the initial string that extend across both spatial dimensions of the lattice. Nonetheless, our error-mitigated estimators from the quantum hardware also give accurate predictions in that regime, with noise-induced violations of local gauge symmetries comparable to finite-bond-dimension tensor-network results.

AI.tldr: The paper implements a (2+1)D U(1) quantum link model on an IBM quantum computer using up to 112 qubits, modeling confining string dynamics via dual height variables and heavy-hexagonal lattice geometry. Results from digital quantum simulations and error-mitigated quantum hardware show good agreement with tensor-network calculations and thermal averages.
AI.motivation: To use the (2+1)D U(1) pure gauge theory (which always confines with non-zero string tension) as a testing ground for quantum computing methods to study string dynamics in confining gauge theories, particularly real-time dynamics inaccessible to traditional quantum Monte Carlo.
AI.method: Implement a minimal U(1) quantum link model on a quantum computer with qubit degrees of freedom as dual height variables, using a heavy-hexagonal lattice geometry matching IBM hardware to minimize non-adjacent qubit interactions. Perform quantum quenches from initial string states and apply error mitigation.
AI.result: Results from digital quantum simulations (up to 112 qubits) agree well with reference tensor-network calculations at short times and thermal averages at long times. Near the phase transition, large fluctuations of the initial string extend across both spatial dimensions. Error-mitigated quantum hardware gives accurate predictions with noise-induced gauge symmetry violations comparable to finite-bond-dimension tensor-network results.
AI.conclusion: The quantum computing approach effectively simulates real-time string dynamics in confining gauge theories, even near phase transitions, demonstrating viability for studying non-equilibrium phenomena inaccessible to classical methods.

title: Subsystem Quantum Error Correction for Noisy Quantum Metrology
summary: Quantum error correction has been successfully applied to enhance the precision of parameter estimation in the presence of noise. Nonetheless, existing methods require a number of noiseless, controllable ancillae and lack efficient encoding and decoding procedures. In this Letter, we demonstrate that subsystem error correction provides a new direction that can substantially simplify the metrological protocol. We derive general conditions under which subsystem stabilizer codes achieve the Heisenberg limit and show that, for broad classes of noise, this can be realized by syndrome-free protocols using at most a single ancilla qubit. Furthermore, we extend this framework to dynamical error correction and show that Floquet codes can protect time-dependent metrological signals in reaching the Heisenberg limit.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that subsystem error correction, using syndrome-free protocols with at most one ancilla qubit, can achieve the Heisenberg limit for parameter estimation under noise, and extends this to dynamical error correction via Floquet codes.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum metrological protocols require many noiseless, controllable ancillae and lack efficient encoding/decoding procedures. The authors aim to simplify these requirements while still achieving the Heisenberg limit.
AI.method: The authors derive general conditions under which subsystem stabilizer codes achieve the Heisenberg limit, and introduce syndrome-free protocols using at most a single ancilla qubit. They also extend the framework to dynamical error correction using Floquet codes for time-dependent signals.
AI.result: Subsystem error correction can substantially simplify quantum metrology, achieving the Heisenberg limit with minimal ancilla overhead (at most one qubit) for broad noise classes. Floquet codes can protect time-dependent signals at the Heisenberg limit.
AI.conclusion: Subsystem error correction offers a practical and efficient pathway for Heisenberg-limited quantum metrology under noise, with dramatically reduced resource requirements.

title: Optimized Quantum States for Sensing in the Presence of Loss and Phase Noise
comment: The build is 8 pages, 5 figures (3 in the body, 2 in the End Matter)
summary: Squeezed vacuum lets gravitational-wave detectors and other quantum sensors surpass the standard quantum limit, and is optimal in the loss-limited regime; phase noise breaks this optimality. Numerically optimizing the quantum Fisher information across the loss and phase-noise landscape, we identify non-Gaussian states that outperform any Gaussian state. These fall into three classes: Fock-like, cubic-phase-like, and states with discrete rotational symmetry. Limiting the average number of photons in the input state to $\bar{n}=5$, with $1-η= 5\%$ photon loss and 200 mrad phase noise, the non-Gaussian advantage reaches up to 2.2 dB. Furthermore, we observe that the non-Gaussian advantage can persist even when the measurement strategy is homodyne detection.

AI.tldr: Non-Gaussian states (Fock-like, cubic-phase-like, discrete-symmetry) outperform Gaussian squeezed vacuum in quantum metrology under concurrent loss and phase noise, achieving up to 2.2 dB advantage at $\bar{n}=5$, 5% loss, and 200 mrad phase noise.
AI.motivation: Squeezed vacuum is optimal for quantum sensing in loss-limited regimes, but phase noise breaks this optimality. The authors aim to identify states that can outperform Gaussian states under realistic conditions where both loss and phase noise coexist.
AI.method: Numerically optimize quantum Fisher information across the loss and phase-noise landscape, searching over non-Gaussian states with average photon number constrained to $\bar{n}=5$, under 5% photon loss and 200 mrad phase noise.
AI.result: Three classes of non-Gaussian states outperform Gaussian states: Fock-like, cubic-phase-like, and states with discrete rotational symmetry. The non-Gaussian advantage reaches up to 2.2 dB, and persists even under homodyne detection.
AI.conclusion: Non-Gaussian states offer a practical advantage for quantum-enhanced sensing in realistic noisy environments, and this advantage is robust enough to survive suboptimal measurement strategies like homodyne detection.

title: Quantum Dynamics from Lax Pair Theory: A Reconstruction from Spectrum Preservation
summary: We reconstruct unitary quantum dynamics from a minimal axiomatic foundation built on Hilbert-space observables and isospectral evolution. The only dynamical assumption is that physical time evolution is a continuous one-parameter flow of Hermitian observables that preserves their spectra, i.e. the possible outcomes of measurement. We show that this assumption is already sufficient to force the Lax form of quantum dynamics. The Heisenberg equation, the time-dependent and time-independent Schrödinger equations, conservation laws, and good quantum numbers then follow as theorems rather than postulates. In this formulation, Lax pair theory supplies the missing dynamical bridge between the measurement structure of a Hilbert space and standard quantum evolution: the Hamiltonian is not assumed, but emerges as the generator required for an isospectral observable flow.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that starting from only the assumption that quantum observables evolve via continuous, spectrum-preserving flows, the full standard quantum dynamics (Heisenberg/Schrödinger equations, conservation laws, etc.) can be derived as theorems via Lax pair theory, with the Hamiltonian emerging as the necessary generator rather than being assumed.
AI.motivation: To reconstruct unitary quantum dynamics from a minimal axiomatic foundation, eliminating the need to postulate the Hamiltonian or the Schrödinger/Heisenberg equations a priori.
AI.method: The authors assume only that time evolution is a continuous one-parameter flow of Hermitian observables preserving their spectra (isospectral evolution). They then apply Lax pair theory to show that this spectral conservation forces the Lax form, from which the Heisenberg equation, Schrödinger equations, and conservation laws follow as theorems.
AI.result: The isospectral assumption alone suffices to derive the Lax form of quantum dynamics, the Heisenberg equation, both time-dependent and time-independent Schrödinger equations, conservation laws, and good quantum numbers—all as consequences rather than postulates.
AI.conclusion: The Hamiltonian is not an input assumption but emerges as the generator required for an isospectral observable flow, meaning Lax pair theory provides the missing dynamical bridge between Hilbert-space measurement structure and standard quantum evolution.

title: Topological Quantum Interferometry
summary: Structured light provides high-dimensional Hilbert spaces holding tremendous potential for fundamental quantum optics and quantum technologies. However, existing characterization methods, like Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference, typically assume perfectly tuned conditions, overlooking the geometric physics governing spatial mode evolution. Here, we establish topological quantum interferometry driven by an interaction-based geometric phase, the exchange Berry phase (BPX). Our formalism generalizes $q$-plate state generation and characterization to arbitrary topological charges and (de)tuning conditions, demonstrating that BPX acts as a geometric marker governing spatial interference. We show BPX serves as a deterministic control parameter, decomposing two-photon spatial patterns into geometry-dictated fundamental modes. This mapping reveals topological invariants and phase singularities that function as a non-tomographic witness for state dimensionality estimation, circumventing full-state reconstruction. Being device-independent and highly scalable, this approach enables scalable high-dimensional characterization and topologically protected state selection, with direct applicability to quantum metrology and high-capacity quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes topological quantum interferometry using the exchange Berry phase (BPX) as a geometric marker for characterizing high-dimensional structured light in quantum optics, enabling non-tomographic dimensionality estimation and topologically protected state selection.
AI.motivation: Existing characterization methods like Hong-Ou-Mandel interference assume perfectly tuned conditions and overlook the geometric physics governing spatial mode evolution in high-dimensional structured light systems.
AI.method: The paper generalizes q-plate state generation and characterization to arbitrary topological charges and (de)tuning conditions, using the exchange Berry phase (BPX) as a deterministic control parameter that decomposes two-photon spatial patterns into geometry-dictated fundamental modes.
AI.result: BPX reveals topological invariants and phase singularities that function as a non-tomographic witness for state dimensionality estimation, circumventing the need for full-state reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: This device-independent, scalable approach enables high-dimensional characterization and topologically protected state selection, with direct applicability to quantum metrology and high-capacity quantum networks.

title: Sparse positive maps on qutrits with exact nondecomposability thresholds and PPT-entanglement transitions
summary: We study a family of sparse positive maps on qutrits for which positivity, decomposability, and PPT entanglement can all be analysed explicitly. The block structure of the associated Choi matrices reduces positivity to a Hermitian biquadratic form and leads to exact positivity boundaries for three representative parametric families. For the same families we determine the exact transition between decomposable and non-decomposable maps and construct associated PPT states of two classes. The first consists of witness-adapted deformations naturally tied to the non-decomposability analysis. The second consists of analytically tractable families whose full PPT-entangled branch is detected by fixed positive maps, yielding exact thresholds between separability and bound entanglement. For the trace-preserving subclass, we further compare positivity with a recent eigenvalue bound for 2-positive maps, thereby making the gap between positivity and higher-order positivity fully explicit within this family.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes sparse positive maps on qutrits, determining exact boundaries for positivity, decomposability, and PPT entanglement. It constructs two classes of PPT entangled states and derives exact separability-to-bound-entanglement thresholds, while also quantifying the gap between positivity and 2-positivity for trace-preserving subclasses.
AI.motivation: To understand the structure of positive maps on qutrits and their relationship to entanglement detection, particularly the transition between decomposable and non-decomposable maps and the exact thresholds for bound entanglement.
AI.method: The block structure of Choi matrices reduces positivity to a Hermitian biquadratic form. The study examines three representative parametric families of sparse positive maps, with exact positivity boundaries and decomposability transitions derived analytically. Two classes of PPT entangled states are constructed: witness-adapted deformations and analytically tractable families detected by fixed positive maps.
AI.result: Exact positivity boundaries determined for three parametric families. Exact decomposable/non-decomposable transition boundaries identified. Two classes of PPT entangled states constructed with exact separability-to-bound-entanglement thresholds. For trace-preserving subclasses, the gap between positivity and 2-positivity is made fully explicit via comparison with an eigenvalue bound.
AI.conclusion: The exact analytical treatment of these sparse positive map families provides precise insights into the structure of positive maps, their decomposability, and their ability to detect bound entanglement in qutrit systems.

title: Robust Generation of Topological Biphoton Mode via Adiabatic Passage
summary: Topological waveguide arrays support robust mode propagation in the presence of fabrication imperfections, providing a significant advantage for on-chip quantum information processing. However, this robustness does not fully extend to nonlinear biphoton generation. Structural disorder can enhance the excitation of non-topological biphoton modes during nonlinear interactions, which degrades the quantum properties of the generated state. To overcome this limitation, we propose an adiabatic passage that connects an isolated site to a topological defect array. By initiating the nonlinear process in a strongly isolated regime, nonlinear coupling to unwanted modes is effectively suppressed, thereby preserving the Schmidt number of the generated state. The subsequent adiabatic connection facilitates the high fidelity transfer of the generated biphoton into the topological biphoton mode. Our numerical simulations demonstrate that, unlike conventional topological structures, the adiabatic scheme maintains both high biphoton fidelity and a unit Schmidt number in the presence of waveguide gap disorder. Furthermore, we show that this robustness extends to path entangled NOON states, achieving a near-unity quantum interference visibility. Our approach provides a practical design strategy for disorder-tolerant integrated quantum photonic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adiabatic passage scheme connecting an isolated site to a topological defect array to suppress nonlinear coupling to unwanted biphoton modes induced by disorder, preserving Schmidt number and fidelity in biphoton generation and NOON states.
AI.motivation: Topological waveguide arrays are robust against fabrication imperfections for mode propagation, but this robustness does not fully extend to nonlinear biphoton generation because structural disorder can enhance excitation of non-topological biphoton modes, degrading quantum state properties.
AI.method: An adiabatic passage that connects an isolated site to a topological defect array is proposed, where the nonlinear process is initiated in a strongly isolated regime to suppress unwanted mode coupling, followed by adiabatic connection to transfer the biphoton into the topological mode with high fidelity.
AI.result: Numerical simulations demonstrate that the adiabatic scheme maintains both high biphoton fidelity and a unit Schmidt number under waveguide gap disorder, unlike conventional topological structures. Robustness also extends to path-entangled NOON states with near-unity quantum interference visibility.
AI.conclusion: The adiabatic approach provides a practical design strategy for disorder-tolerant integrated quantum photonic devices, overcoming the limitations of topological protection for nonlinear quantum processes.

title: QMCtwin: Master-Equation Simulation of Syndrome Statistics Beyond Pauli Noise
summary: As quantum error correction moves toward large-scale experimental implementations, decoder performance increasingly depends on how faithfully hardware noise is translated into syndrome statistics. Standard stabilizer workflows achieve scalability by replacing device dynamics with stochastic Pauli or detector-error models, but this compression can discard coherent phase information, nonunital drift, continuous-time effects of always-on couplings, and correlations generated by simultaneous Hamiltonian and dissipative evolution. Here we present QMCtwin, a sign-problem-suppressed quantum Monte Carlo framework for master-equation simulation of QEC circuits, and apply it to a full syndrome-extraction round of a distance-$7$ rotated surface code with $97$ physical qubits. The open-system model includes realistic superconducting-device noise mechanisms such as relaxation, pure dephasing, coherent gate miscalibration, residual $ZZ$ crosstalk, and drive-qubit detuning. By directly estimating syndrome observables from the QMC-generated stochastic density matrix estimator, we compare the master-equation dynamics with their Pauli-twirled Clifford simulation counterparts. QMCtwin predicts syndrome-extraction biases and correlations between syndromes and proxies of logical-string-parity that are absent or strongly suppressed in the stochastic Pauli description. We introduce information-theoretic diagnostics that further quantify how information concerning syndromes versus string-parity proxies differs between the realistic master-equation simulation and the corresponding Pauli-twirled model. These results show that QMC-based master-equation digital twins can expose noise features hidden by conventional Pauli/Clifford noise models and provide a practical path toward more accurate decoder-facing syndrome models.

AI.tldr: QMCtwin is a sign-problem-suppressed quantum Monte Carlo framework for master-equation simulation of QEC circuits. Applied to a distance-7 rotated surface code with 97 qubits, it reveals syndrome-extraction biases and correlations absent in standard Pauli/Clifford noise models, demonstrating that QMC-based digital twins can expose hidden noise features for more accurate decoder models.
AI.motivation: Standard stabilizer workflows compress hardware noise into stochastic Pauli or detector-error models, discarding coherent phase information, nonunital drift, continuous-time always-on coupling effects, and Hamiltonian-dissipative correlations. This motivates a more faithful simulation framework to capture noise features missed by conventional models.
AI.method: QMCtwin uses a sign-problem-suppressed quantum Monte Carlo method to simulate master-equation dynamics of QEC circuits. It directly estimates syndrome observables from a stochastic density matrix estimator and compares them against Pauli-twirled Clifford simulations. The model includes relaxation, pure dephasing, coherent gate miscalibration, residual ZZ crosstalk, and drive-qubit detuning.
AI.result: QMCtwin predicts syndrome-extraction biases and correlations between syndromes and logical-string-parity proxies that are absent or strongly suppressed in the stochastic Pauli description. Information-theoretic diagnostics quantify discrepancies in syndrome vs. string-parity proxy information between the master-equation and Pauli-twirled models.
AI.conclusion: QMC-based master-equation digital twins can expose noise features hidden by conventional Pauli/Clifford noise models and provide a practical path toward more accurate decoder-facing syndrome models.

title: Random Local Stabilizer Codes in Three Dimensions without String or Self-Similar Fractal Logical Operators
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures. Repository for data: https://github.com/hanyanphysics/QTRCC
summary: Quantum error-correcting codes (QECs) are essential components quantum computation and have deep connections to quantum phases of matter. A key obstruction to passive self-correcting QECs is the presence of string logical operators, which can generate logical errors through constant-energy-barrier processes. Haah's Codes (fracton codes) showed that three-dimensional stabilizer codes can forbid such string logical operators, but their translation-invariant structure supports self-similar fractal logical operators with a logarithmic energy barrier. We introduce the qutrit random cubic codes, a family of local qutrit Calderbank-Shor-Steane stabilizer Hamiltonians with similar cube-check structure as Haah's Code 1 but built from spatially varying stabilizers. We prove that these models retain the no-string property and numerically observe that they have properties distinct from translation-invariant fracton codes: the smallest ground-state degeneracy exponent is $k=2$ for odd $L$ and $k=4$ for even $L$; noncontractible plane-logical operators span the entire logical space; and charge-push diagnostics show that the self-similar fractal operators are absent. These results demonstrate that constrained randomness can fundamentally change the nature of stabilizer codes and improve their self-correction properties. They further point to broader families of quantum error-correcting codes and quantum phases beyond canonical topological and fracton orders.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces qutrit random cubic codes—a family of 3D local stabilizer Hamiltonians with spatially varying cube-check structure—that retain the no-string property of Haah's codes but eliminate self-similar fractal logical operators, leading to distinct ground-state degeneracy scaling and improved self-correction properties.
AI.motivation: String logical operators in quantum error-correcting codes can generate logical errors via constant-energy-barrier processes, obstructing passive self-correction. While Haah's (fracton) codes forbid string operators, they still support self-similar fractal logical operators with logarithmic energy barriers. The authors seek to design codes that suppress both string and fractal operators to improve self-correction.
AI.method: The authors construct qutrit random cubic codes: 3D local qutrit CSS stabilizer Hamiltonians with cube-check interactions analogous to Haah's Code 1, but with spatially varying (random) stabilizer coefficients. They analytically prove the no-string property and numerically study ground-state degeneracy, logical operator structure, and charge-push diagnostics.
AI.result: The codes retain the no-string property. Numerical results show: (1) minimal ground-state degeneracy exponent k=2 for odd L and k=4 for even L; (2) noncontractible plane-logical operators span the entire logical space; (3) charge-push diagnostics indicate the absence of self-similar fractal operators.
AI.conclusion: Constrained randomness fundamentally alters the nature of stabilizer codes, eliminating fractal operators and improving self-correction. This points to broader families of QECs and quantum phases beyond canonical topological and fracton orders.

title: Purity and bound energy in ancilla-assisted work extraction
summary: We investigate ancilla-assisted work extraction in quantum batteries from the perspective of bound energy and purity. We show that the bound energy of the reduced system provides a tight upper bound to the daemonic gain and that this bound is saturated for globally pure system--ancilla states. Motivated by this relation, we introduce a purity-based gain that qualitatively predicts the daemonic gain without requiring explicit optimization over measurements. We further introduce a protocol to analyze the role of dissipation and intrinsic interactions on daemonic gain. Under a collective environment, dissipation can dynamically generate and stabilize finite daemonic gain through environment-induced correlations. In interacting systems, level crossings and spectral restructuring strongly modify the attainable gain through their influence on the accessible bound energy. Our results demonstrate that daemonic gain is governed not only by correlations, but also by the spectral structure of the underlying Hamiltonian and information loss captured by bound energy and purity.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates ancilla-assisted work extraction (daemonic gain) in quantum batteries, showing it is bounded by the bound energy of the reduced system and saturated for globally pure states. A purity-based gain predicts this effect without measurement optimization. Under collective dissipation, correlations dynamically generate stable gain, while in interacting systems, spectral restructuring modifies gain via bound energy changes.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of ancilla-assisted work extraction in quantum batteries by connecting daemonic gain to bound energy and purity, and to analyze how dissipation and interactions affect this gain.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of the relationship between daemonic gain and bound energy; introduction of a purity-based gain metric; numerical analysis of a protocol studying dissipation (collective environment) and intrinsic interactions.
AI.result: Bound energy provides a tight upper bound for daemonic gain, saturated for globally pure states. Purity-based gain qualitatively predicts daemonic gain without optimization. Collective dissipation can generate and stabilize finite daemonic gain via environment-induced correlations. Level crossings and spectral restructuring in interacting systems modify attainable gain.
AI.conclusion: Daemonic gain is governed not only by correlations but also by the Hamiltonian's spectral structure and information loss captured by bound energy and purity.

title: QMaxCal: Path-Space Regularization for Open Quantum Control via Girsanov's Theorem
summary: Reliable quantum control in the presence of decoherence requires policies that combat the effect of environmental noise on the controlled dynamics. Open quantum systems under continuous monitoring generate classical measurement records whose drift depends on the noise experienced by the system; the records of two evolutions sharing the same decoherence channels differ only in this drift, so Girsanov's theorem yields a closed-form, differentiable estimator of the KL divergence between their trajectory distributions. We instantiate this estimator with two physically motivated reference measures, yielding two regularizers that both drive the system toward states where the effects of decoherence are minimal: the Wiener KL (KL_W), which is empirically more effective under certain conditions on the noise model, and the drift-variance regularizer (R_DV), which works for all noise models. Both are qualitatively distinct from existing penalties on control fluence or smoothness: they penalize the observable consequences of control on the decoherence channels rather than the control amplitude itself. The regularizers outperform unregularized gradient-based and reinforcement-learning baselines across a range of open quantum systems -- including single- and multi-qubit benchmarks and a multi-qubit chain calibrated to a published snapshot of the IBM Kingston processor -- along several axes of evaluation: final-state fidelity, robustness to mismatch in the assumed noise model (gains grow from +17 pp at training noise to +27 pp under 2.5x noise mismatch), and occupation of forbidden states. The regularizers reduce infidelity by up to 50%, with ~16% gains on the calibrated IBM Kingston chain.
